name: Anchoring Bias
description: Initial exposure to a number or value ('anchor') skews subsequent judgments and valuations toward that anchor, even when the anchor is arbitrary or irrelevant.
design_relevance_note: Common in pricing displays (showing a high 'original price' next to a discount), estimation tasks, and form defaults that subtly bias user input.
myth_risk_note: Strong empirical backing exists with direct replication studies in large samples finding consistent effects across diverse contexts; rated low rather than none since this re-review found a clinical-decision-making systematic review worth noting as additional context, not a genuine dispute.
prevalence_note: Core Kahneman/Tversky concept, taught in essentially every behavioral-economics-for-design curriculum and referenced constantly in pricing/negotiation UX writing.

findings.description: Initial valuations of products/experiences are strongly influenced by arbitrary anchors (e.g., digits from a person's own social security number), yet subsequent valuations remain internally consistent relative to quality/quantity differences — creating an illusion of stable underlying preferences that isn't actually present; the effect persists with market experience and isn't reduced by market forces.
findings.source_title: "Coherent Arbitrariness": Stable Demand Curves Without Stable Preferences

findings.description: Three heuristics — representativeness, availability, and anchoring/adjustment — are used in judgment under uncertainty; each is economical and usually effective, but each produces systematic, predictable biases.
findings.source_title: Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases

applications.title: Amazon's 'was price' strikethrough reference pricing
applications.description: Amazon displays a struck-through reference ('was') price beside the current price across product listings -- the higher figure anchors perception of the current price as a discount, even when the comparison price itself is disputed.
applications.ethical_note: This is the anchoring application most directly implicated in this graph's own dark-patterns literature: a consumer-advocacy group and a real regulatory standard (FTC guidance on former-price comparisons) treat this specific pattern as a live deception risk, not a neutral persuasion technique. The anchor here isn't just 'a higher number makes the lower number look good' in the abstract -- it's specifically alleged that the higher number itself may not be a genuine prior price, which is what turns ordinary anchoring into a contested, potentially regulator-relevant practice. This claim is now nearly a decade old (2017) -- flagged via date_observed as due for re-verification against current Amazon practice, not presented as necessarily still accurate today.

applications.title: BIT's field trial with bet365: removing high deposit-limit anchors cut chosen limits by ~45%
applications.description: The UK's Behavioural Insights Team ran a randomized field trial with gambling operator bet365 testing deposit-limit-tool designs: a control group saw the industry-standard dropdown with anchors as high as GBP100,000, a second group saw only lower anchors (up to GBP250), and a third group set a limit via a free-text box with no anchors shown at all. Removing the high anchors from view reduced the size of customers' chosen deposit limits by an estimated ~45%.
applications.ethical_note: A rare case where anchoring is deliberately used against the industry's own default framing to reduce consumer harm rather than to increase spend -- the opposite direction from most anchoring applications in this corpus (e.g. the iPad launch, Amazon's 'was' price), included specifically to show the same mechanism can be turned toward protecting users, not just persuading them to spend more.

applications.title: Consumers' Checkbook's 2022 tracking study: false 'was' prices rampant across major physical and online retailers
applications.description: The nonprofit Consumers' Checkbook tracked prices of the same items at 25 major retailers over 33 weeks in 2022, finding that at eight of the companies, more than half the tracked items were offered at false discounts (an inflated 'was' price used as the anchor) nearly every week -- Foot Locker's tracked items were 'on sale' 98% of the time. Only two of the 25 retailers, Apple and Costco, were found to offer consistently legitimate discounts from genuinely established prices.
applications.ethical_note: A large, multi-retailer, longitudinal study directly measuring a widespread deceptive-anchoring practice across the physical and online retail industry, not a single company's isolated choice -- reinforces this corpus's existing single-retailer anchoring examples (Amazon, the iPad launch) with evidence that the underlying tactic is an industry norm rather than an exception, and specifically identifies the practice as illegal-but-rarely-policed in the U.S.

applications.title: JCPenney's 2012 removal of price anchors ('Fair and Square' pricing) led to a sales collapse
applications.description: In 2011-2012, new JCPenney CEO Ron Johnson (formerly of Apple) replaced the retailer's coupon-and-markdown pricing model with 'everyday low prices' -- removing the inflated reference prices and discount anchors customers had come to expect. Rather than being welcomed as more honest pricing, the change was followed by a steep sales decline, and the strategy was reversed within about a year.
applications.ethical_note: An instructive counter-case to this corpus's other anchoring examples: removing a manipulative anchor entirely, even in the name of pricing honesty, can backfire commercially if customers have been conditioned to expect and value the anchor-and-discount ritual itself -- a real illustration that the ethics and the effectiveness of anchoring are separate questions, not the same one.

applications.title: Steve Jobs anchoring the original iPad's price against a rumored $999
applications.description: At the 2010 iPad launch keynote, Steve Jobs first displayed pundits' rumored price of $999 on screen, held it there, then revealed the actual price of $499 with the higher figure visually 'crushed' by the lower one -- using the inflated rumor as a deliberate anchor to make the real price feel cheap by comparison.
applications.ethical_note: A deliberate anchor used in a live public presentation to shape price perception -- not deceptive in the sense of a fabricated reference price (the $999 figure was genuinely the media's own pre-launch speculation, not an invented strawman), but still a calculated framing choice designed to make $499 feel like a bargain regardless of the device's independent value. Sits closer to persuasion than manipulation since the anchor was real, publicly-sourced pundit speculation rather than a fabricated number, but the intent to exploit the contrast is explicit and worth naming as such.
